subject: Biotechnology
title: Cas9 and Beyond
description: A 60-second lesson on Cas9 and Beyond.

hook.text: Cas9 was first — but the CRISPR toolkit now includes a dozen different enzymes, each with unique talents.

buildup.text: Cas12a cuts with staggered ends and uses a shorter guide — better for multiplexing many targets at once.

discovery.text: Cas13 targets RNA instead of DNA — it can knock down gene expression without altering the genome permanently.

twist.text: Dead Cas9 cuts nothing — instead it sits on DNA and blocks or activates genes. Editing without cutting.

climax.text: New CRISPR systems from uncultured bacteria keep appearing — nature's diversity fuels the next generation of editors.

punchline.text: Cas9 opened the door — its cousins are furnishing the house.

quiz.question: What makes Cas13 different from Cas9?
options: Cas13 cuts protein instead of nucleic acid
Cas13 targets RNA instead of DNA, allowing gene knockdown without permanent genome changes
Cas13 works only in plant cells, not animal cells

details.summary: Cas9 was the first CRISPR nuclease widely adopted for genome editing, but the toolkit has expanded dramatically to include Cas12 for DNA detection, Cas13 for RNA targeting, and compact Cas variants that fit in viral vectors for gene therapy delivery.
details.whyItMatters: Different Cas proteins enable different applications beyond simple gene cutting. RNA-targeting Cas13 allows reversible gene knockdown, Cas12 powers rapid diagnostics, and small Cas proteins solve the delivery challenge that limits gene therapy
takeaways: Cas12 enables sensitive nucleic acid detection in diagnostic platforms
Cas13 targets RNA for reversible gene silencing without altering DNA
Compact Cas proteins fit inside AAV vectors for direct gene therapy delivery

faq.question: Why do we need CRISPR proteins beyond Cas9?
faq.answer: Cas9 cuts DNA at specific sites but is too large for some delivery methods, cannot target RNA, and only recognizes specific PAM sequences. Cas12 recognizes different PAMs expanding targetable sites. Cas13 targets RNA reversibly. CasX and CasPhi are small enough for AAV delivery.

faq.question: How does Cas12 enable rapid disease diagnostics?
faq.answer: Cas12 exhibits collateral cleavage activity, cutting nearby single-stranded DNA after binding its target. Diagnostic systems use this to detect specific pathogen sequences: when Cas12 finds its target, it cuts fluorescent reporter molecules, producing a visible or measurable signal within minutes.
